These studies were led by the teams of Prof. Baile Zhang at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, and Prof. Jianhua Jiang at the University of Science and Technology of China, respectively. Prof. Xue-Jia Yu from the School of Physics at the Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo (EIT), served as a co-corresponding author on both papers and provided key theoretical guidance in the related experimental collaborations.\n\n[L27] Kubernetes Metrics Guide from Datadog\n[L28] Kubernetes Metrics Guide from Datadog\n[L29] Datadog\n[L30] Datadog\n·\n[L32] Sponsored\n[L33] call to action icon\n\n[L35] Subscribe to our newsletter for the latest sci-tech news updates.\n\n[L37] Topology: A robust framework protected by topological invariants\n[L38] To understand the significance of this work, we first need to discuss the concept of topology.\n\n[L40] In the conventional picture of physics, the states of matter are determined by symmetry. For example, the transition of water into ice and the magnetization of iron are both results of symmetry breaking. However, the discovery of topological phases of matter fundamentally changed this understanding (recognized by the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physics).\n\n[L42] Topology focuses on global properties of objects that remain unchanged under continuous deformation. As an analogy, a coffee mug and a doughnut are considered equivalent from the perspective of topology: the handle of the mug can be continuously deformed into a hole, and as long as the object is not torn or glued, the number of holes remains unchanged.\n\n[L44] Top-10 Ranked University - Georgia Tech - 2-Year Degree Program\n[L45] Top-10 Ranked University - Georgia Tech - 2-Year Degree Program\n[L46] info.pe.gatech.edu\n·\n[L48] Sponsored\n[L49] call to action icon\n\n[L51] This quantized robustness gives topological phases of matter a natural advantage: exceptional stability. The quantum Hall effect, topological insulators, and other representative topological materials rely on the protection of global topological invariants. Even in the presence of symmetry-preserving impurities and perturbations, their conducting edge states remain robust.\n\n[L53] However, this protection has a prerequisite—the bulk state of the material must possess an energy gap. Once the energy gap closes, the topological invariant is no longer well defined, and the edge states disappear accordingly. Therefore, the scientific community has long held the principle that topological phases of matter are inherently associated with the existence of an energy gap.\n\n[L55] Criticality: Where distinct systems exhibit universal behavior\n[L56] In contrast to the \"rigidity\" of topology is the critical point in continuous phase transitions—for example, the transition of water into vapor at the boiling point and the loss of magnetism at the Curie point. Near a critical point, the energy gap of a system completely closes, microscopic details are smoothed out, and only collective behaviors at long wavelengths remain.\n\n[L58] Download AWS Lambda Cheatsheet\n[L59] Download AWS Lambda Cheatsheet\n[L60] Datadog\n·\n[L62] Sponsored\n[L63] call to action icon\n\n[L65] At this point, materials with very different microscopic properties can exhibit exactly the same critical exponents and belong to the same universality class. This is one of the most fascinating discoveries in physics (recognized by the 1982 Nobel Prize in Physics): at critical points, seemingly diverse systems can converge into the same universal description.\n\n[L67] However, this framework appears almost entirely incompatible with topological phases of matter. Critical points are gapless, whereas topology requires an energy gap; criticality is continuous, whereas topology is characterized by discrete invariants. For decades, these two fundamental pillars of physics were regarded as two separate domains that developed independently with limited overlap.\n\n[L69] From a long-standing boundary to a new frontier\n[L70] \"Can topology survive at a critical point?\" This question was once considered a fundamental challenge to the conventional understanding of topology in physics. In recent years, a small number of theoretical physicists, including Prof. Xue-Jia Yu, have begun to systematically explore this possibility. Prof. Yu and collaborators have carried out a series of theoretical studies in this direction.\n\n[L72] In 2022, they proposed a theoretical classification theory for topology at quantum critical points; In 2024, they proposed a generalized topological bulk–edge correspondence applicable to critical points; In 2026, they further extended the related theory to nonequilibrium dynamics. In addition, Prof. Xue-Jia Yu collaborated with Prof. Limei Xu from Peking University and Chair Professor Hai-Qing Lin from Zhejiang University. Together, they were invited to publish the first comprehensive review article on this topic in the journal Physics Reports. This review article systematically summarizes the complete theoretical framework of critical topology.\n\n[L74] The theory was ready, but experimental realization remained difficult\n[L75] Although the theoretical framework had gradually become clearer, experimental realization had remained challenging. To realize critical topology in a real physical system, researchers need to precisely tune the system to a critical point, where the bulk state becomes completely gapless. At the same time, they must detect the signatures of topological edge states against strong fluctuations and background noise.\n\n[L77] This challenge is extremely demanding: it is almost like stopping a high-speed train precisely at the edge of a cliff while still measuring a tiny particle of dust on the wheel. Therefore, for many years, the exciting predictions of critical topology remained only in theoretical studies and numerical simulations.\n\n[L79] Theoretical contributions underlie two independent experiments\n[L80] This situation has now been changed. Prof. Xue-Jia Yu collaborated with the experimental teams of Prof. Baile Zhang from Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, and Prof. Jianhua Jiang from the University of Science and Technology of China. Using acoustic metamaterials as an artificial platform, the teams experimentally observed critical topological phenomena and achieved a breakthrough from theoretical prediction to experimental realization.\n\n[L82] The two experiments adopted completely different design strategies and measurement approaches. As a co-corresponding author of both Nature papers, Prof. Yu provided key support in theoretical modeling, mechanism interpretation, and analysis of the physical picture related to the experiments.\n\n[L84] In the first study (\"Observation of critical topological phase transition\"), Based on the theoretical framework proposed by Prof. Xue-Jia Yu and further developed together with collaborators, the experimental team successfully observed topological zero-energy modes and π modes at a one-dimensional Floquet critical point, experimentally realizing the critical topological phenomena.\n\n[L86] In the second study (\"Experimental observation of critical topology\"), the experimental team adopted the generalized Li–Haldane bulk–edge correspondence proposed by Prof. Xue-Jia Yu. Through experimental measurements of the entanglement spectrum, the team achieved the observation of one-dimensional and two-dimensional critical topological phenomena.\n\n[L88] Two papers, two independent experiments, and the same theoretical origin—the team of Prof. Xue-Jia Yu at EIT, served as the core theoretical support underlying both studies.\n\n[L90] From 'impossible' to experimental realization\n[L91] These two independent Nature studies provide the first experimental evidence in real physical systems that: topology can survive even when the energy gap closes; critical universal behavior and topological properties can coexist. These findings not only transform critical topology from a theoretical concept into experimental reality, but also open new possibilities for future studies of topological quantum computation, novel acoustic devices, and nonequilibrium topological phases of matter.\n\n[L93] Topology and criticality, two concepts once considered incompatible, have finally met in the laboratory. The main theoretical force behind this convergence came from Prof. Xue-Jia Yu's team at the Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo.\n\n[L95] More information: Baile Zhang, Observation of critical topological phase transition, Nature (2026). Here I show that the same expression has a much simpler geometric meaning: it is exactly the volume fraction of a spherical body lying outside the threshold radius\n\\[\nr_c=\\frac{v_{\\rm crit}}{\\omega}=\\frac{R}{x}.\n\\]\nFor rotational dynamics, however, volume is not the relevant measure. Angular momentum is weighted by distance from the rotation axis. For a uniform-density spherical body, the corresponding moment-of-inertia participation fraction is\n\\[\nP_I(x)=\\left(1-x^{-5}\\right)H(x-1).\n\\]\nEliminating the threshold variable gives the parameter-free relation\n\\[\n\\boxed{P_I=1-(1-D_V)^{5/3}}.\n\\]\nIn the thin-shell limit,\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{P_I}{D_V}\\rightarrow\\frac53,\\qquad \\frac{D_V}{P_I}\\rightarrow\\frac35}.\n\\]\nThis 3→5 exponent shift is the finite-core correction required when an archived line/shell threshold model is used to describe a rotational event. It provides a direct observational discriminator in glitches for which both radiative-shell response and angular-momentum participation can be estimated. The relation is proposed as a test on systems such as PSR J0205+6449, where short-term pulsed gamma-ray changes have been reported following a glitch, and on newly glitching systems such as PSR J1637−4642.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Problem\n\nPulsar glitches are abrupt increases in rotation frequency. Standard models generally involve angular-momentum exchange among the crust, superfluid components, pinned vortices, and elastic or magnetic stresses. SAT developed a separate geometric-threshold picture in which a radial portion of the rotating body crosses a critical condition and participates in a rapid structural transition.\n\nOne archived SAT paper wrote\n\\[\nD_V(x)=1-x^{-3},\\qquad x\\ge1,\n\\]\nand then identified that quantity directly with both decoupled material fraction and fractional spin jump.\n\nThat identification mixes two different measures.\n\nA volume fraction weights material by \\(r^2dr\\). Rotational inertia weights the same material by \\(r^4dr\\). A finite-radius worldtube/shell description therefore requires distinguishing them.\n\nThis paper performs that lift without adding any new force or substrate.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Archived threshold law as ordinary geometry\n\nLet a star of radius \\(R\\) rotate with angular velocity \\(\\omega\\). Suppose a local threshold is crossed where tangential speed exceeds a critical value \\(v_{\\rm crit}\\).\n\nThe boundary radius is determined by\n\\[\n\\omega r_c=v_{\\rm crit},\n\\]\nso\n\\[\nr_c=\\frac{v_{\\rm crit}}{\\omega}.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\\[\nx=\\frac{\\omega R}{v_{\\rm crit}}.\n\\]\nThen\n\\[\n\\frac{r_c}{R}=x^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nFor a uniform sphere, the fraction of the stellar volume outside \\(r_c\\) is\n\\[\nD_V\n=\\frac{R^3-r_c^3}{R^3}\n=1-\\left(\\frac{r_c}{R}\\right)^3\n=1-x^{-3}.\n\\]\n\nThus the archived cubic law is not intrinsically fractal or lattice-specific. It is the ordinary volume fraction of a spherical threshold shell.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Rotational lift: exponent 3 becomes exponent 5\n\nThe moment of inertia of a uniform spherical shell element about a fixed diameter is\n\\[\ndI=\\frac{8\\pi}{3}\\rho r^4\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\\[\nI(<R)=\\frac{8\\pi\\rho}{15}R^5.\n\\]\n\nThe moment of inertia residing outside \\(r_c\\) is\n\\[\nI_{\\rm shell}\n=\\frac{8\\pi\\rho}{15}\\left(R^5-r_c^5\\right).\n\\]\n\nTherefore the fractional rotational participation is\n\\[\nP_I\n=\\frac{I_{\\rm shell}}{I_{\\rm total}}\n=1-\\left(\\frac{r_c}{R}\\right)^5\n=1-x^{-5}.\n\\]\n\nThis is the simplest finite-core correction to the archived threshold model.\n\nThe distinction is physical rather than semantic:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{volume support}\\propto r^3,\\qquad\n\\text{rotational support}\\propto r^5.}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n## 4. Parameter-free observable relation\n\nBecause\n\\[\n1-D_V=x^{-3},\n\\]\nwe have\n\\[\nx^{-5}=(x^{-3})^{5/3}=(1-D_V)^{5/3}.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\\[\n\\boxed{P_I=1-(1-D_V)^{5/3}}.\n\\]\n\nConversely,\n\\[\n\\boxed{D_V=1-(1-P_I)^{3/5}}.\n\\]\n\nNo critical velocity appears in these relations. No SAT projection constant appears. The relation follows only from a common threshold radius and uniform spherical geometry.\n\nFor a thin shell,\n\\[\nD_V\\simeq 3\\frac{\\delta r}{R},\n\\qquad\nP_I\\simeq 5\\frac{\\delta r}{R},\n\\]\nso\n\\[\n\\boxed{P_I\\simeq\\frac53D_V}.\n\\]\n\n### Numerical predictions\n\nIf the same threshold boundary controls both an approximately volume-weighted radiative response and the rotationally participating shell:\n\n| \\(D_V\\) | predicted \\(P_I\\) | \\(P_I/D_V\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| \\(10^{-6}\\) | \\(1.6666661\\times10^{-6}\\) | 1.6666661 |\n| \\(10^{-4}\\) | \\(1.6666111\\times10^{-4}\\) | 1.6666111 |\n| 0.01 | 0.01661105 | 1.66110 |\n| 0.10 | 0.16104722 | 1.61047 |\n| 0.20 | 0.31058090 | 1.55290 |\n| 0.50 | 0.68501974 | 1.37004 |\n| 0.80 | 0.93160096 | 1.16450 |\n\nThe 5/3 thin-shell coefficient is therefore a direct falsification target.\n\n---\n\n## 5. General density profile\n\nA neutron star is not uniform. The geometric statement survives with the density profile made explicit.\n\nFor density \\(\\rho(r)\\),\n\\[\nD_M(r_c)\n=\n\\frac{\\int_{r_c}^{R}\\rho(r)r^2\\,dr}\n{\\int_{0}^{R}\\rho(r)r^2\\,dr},\n\\]\nwhereas rotational participation is\n\\[\nP_I(r_c)\n=\n\\frac{\\int_{r_c}^{R}\\rho(r)r^4\\,dr}\n{\\int_{0}^{R}\\rho(r)r^4\\,dr}.\n\\]\n\nFor the toy family\n\\[\n\\rho(r)\\propto r^q,\n\\]\none obtains\n\\[\nD_M=1-x^{-(q+3)},\n\\]\nand\n\\[\nP_I=1-x^{-(q+5)}.\n\\]\n\nEliminating \\(x\\),\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_I\n=\n1-(1-D_M)^{(q+5)/(q+3)}\n}.\n\\]\n\nThe uniform result is the \\(q=0\\) member.\n\nThis makes the exponent itself a probe of the radial weighting of the participating region rather than an arbitrary fitting function.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Relation to an observed glitch amplitude\n\nLet the observed fractional spin jump be\n\\[\ng=\\frac{\\Delta\\Omega}{\\Omega}.\n\\]\n\nAngular-momentum conservation gives, schematically,\n\\[\nI_c\\Delta\\Omega\n\\simeq\nI_s\\Delta\\Omega_{\\rm lag},\n\\]\nso\n\\[\ng\n\\simeq\n\\eta\\,\\frac{I_s}{I_c},\n\\qquad\n\\eta\\equiv\\frac{\\Delta\\Omega_{\\rm lag}}{\\Omega}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore \\(g\\) is not generally equal to \\(P_I\\).\n\nThis is the key correction to the archived SAT paper.\n\nThe finite-shell geometry predicts \\(P_I\\). Converting \\(P_I\\) into a glitch amplitude requires the lag released and the coupled inertia of the receiver. Those are standard dynamical quantities and should be measured or modeled rather than hidden inside the geometric fraction.\n\nThe geometry is therefore compatible with vortex, elastic, magnetic, or other mechanisms only if they reproduce the same participating shell boundary.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Target systems\n\n### 7.1 PSR J0205+6449\n\nA 2026 study reports short-term pulsed gamma-ray variations following a glitch in PSR J0205+6449. This system is unusually useful because it provides both a rotational event and a radiative response.\n\nThe proposed test is:\n\n1. estimate or bound a radiative participation fraction \\(D_\\gamma\\);\n2. infer a rotational participation fraction \\(P_I\\) from the timing event using a standard angular-momentum transfer model;\n3. test whether\n   \\[\n   P_I=1-(1-D_\\gamma)^{5/3}\n   \\]\n   is consistent with the data after explicitly modeling the emission weighting.\n\nFailure is informative. It would show either that the radiating region and angular-momentum reservoir do not share the same radial boundary, or that the uniform-shell approximation is inadequate.\n\n### 7.2 PSR J1637−4642\n\nA 2026 discovery paper reports three glitches in the previously quiet pulsar PSR J1637−4642.\n\nThe geometric model predicts that, if all three events are generated by the same threshold family, each event should be describable by a different \\(r_{c,j}\\) but the same radial weighting law:\n\\[\nP_{I,j}=1-\\left(\\frac{r_{c,j}}{R}\\right)^5.\n\\]\n\nIf an independent shell-sensitive observable is available,\n\\[\nD_j=1-\\left(\\frac{r_{c,j}}{R}\\right)^3,\n\\]\nthen all three events must lie on the same curve\n\\[\n\\boxed{P_{I,j}=1-(1-D_j)^{5/3}}.\n\\]\n\nThree events in one star are therefore more discriminating than one event in three stars.\n\n---\n\n## 8. What this says about the archived SAT equations\n\nThe archived \\(1-x^{-3}\\) expression contained a useful geometric construction but attached the wrong physical interpretation to it.\n\nThe correction is not a new SAT mechanism.\n\nIt is the ordinary difference between:\n\n- how much material lies in a shell, and\n- how much rotational inertia lies in that shell.\n\nThe line→worldtube lift therefore produces a concrete repair:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n1-x^{-3}\n\\quad\\longrightarrow\\quad\n1-x^{-5}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhenever the target observable is rotational participation rather than volume participation.\n\nThe old cubic law remains useful for volume-weighted or approximately emissivity-weighted quantities.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Falsification conditions\n\nThe model fails in its minimal form if any of the following occur:\n\n1. a common radial threshold cannot simultaneously describe the rotational and shell-sensitive observables;\n2. the inferred \\(P_I(D)\\) relation is systematically incompatible with the 5/3 law in systems where the uniform-shell approximation should apply;\n3. a realistic density profile cannot repair the discrepancy without introducing an event-by-event arbitrary function;\n4. the observed event requires angular-momentum transfer from a region that is geometrically disjoint from the proposed threshold shell.\n\nThese are failures of the model, not reasons to redefine the observable after the fact.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Prediction\n\nThe immediate quantitative prediction is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_I=1-(1-D)^{5/3}\n}\n\\]\n\nfor a uniform-density spherical threshold shell shared by a volume-weighted response and a rotational participation response.\n\nFor small events,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_I=(1.666666\\ldots)D+O(D^2).\n}\n\\]\n\nEquivalently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=(0.600000\\ldots)P_I+O(P_I^2).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe numbers 5/3 and 3/5 are not fitted.\n\nThey are the dimensional weights of the same finite shell viewed through volume and rotational inertia.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Next calculation\n\nThe next version should replace the uniform density profile with a realistic neutron-star density profile and explicitly fit the three-event PSR J1637−4642 timing data and the PSR J0205+6449 radiative/timing data.\n\nThe calculation should preserve the same radial threshold and ask how much of the 5/3 relation survives after realistic density, oblateness, superfluid reservoir geometry, and emission weighting are introduced.\n\nThat is the needle to thread.\n\"\"\"\n\nreview_packet = r\"\"\"# Hostile peer-review packet\n## Orson Vay, “From Volume Thresholds to Rotational Participation”\n\n### Required question\n\n**Is the new Orson Vay independent-researcher paper better or worse than the paired published/archive paper, and why?**\n\nDo not answer diplomatically. This system is unusually useful because it provides both a rotational event and a radiative response.\n\nThe proposed test is:\n\n1. estimate or bound a radiative participation fraction \\(D_\\gamma\\);\n2. infer a rotational participation fraction \\(P_I\\) from the timing event using a standard angular-momentum transfer model;\n3. test whether\n   \\[\n   P_I=1-(1-D_\\gamma)^{5/3}\n   \\]\n   is consistent with the data after explicitly modeling the emission weighting.\n\nFailure is informative.             "[L1] {\n[L2]   \"content\": \"# The Fundamental Intuitions of SAT\\n\\n> **Historical presentation copy.** This page reformats a source document from the SAT Theory Archive for readability. The wording below is retained from the source; headings and spacing are presentation additions only. Some mechanisms and terminology were later revised or retired.\\n\\n| Field | Value |\\n|---|---|\\n| Source | [`DEV CONVERSATION/FUNDAMENTAL INTUITIONS.txt`](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/DEV%20CONVERSATION/FUNDAMENTAL%20INTUITIONS.txt) |\\n| Phase | Early SAT / foundational statement |\\n| Public milestone | Fundamental Intuitions presented publicly in early 2025 |\\n| Status | Historical foundation; not a statement that every mechanism remains current H(s)H |\\n\\n**Why it is here:** this is one of the clearest compact statements of the construction that became SAT: four-dimensional worldlines treated as filaments, a moving time surface, particles as intersections, and an explicit commitment to preserve successful Standard Model, General Relativity, and Quantum Mechanics structure unless the model is forced elsewhere.\\n\\n[Open the original source in the SAT Archive →](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/DEV%20CONVERSATION/FUNDAMENTAL%20INTUITIONS.txt)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## SAT — Scalar-Angular-Torsion Theory\\n\\n### The Fundamental Intuitions of SAT\\n\\n**0th:** The \\\"real world\\\" is the world of particle worldlines plotted in four dimensions; it is a hypercomplex tangled \\\"Zottenwelt\\\" of worldlines--SAT calls these worldlines *filaments* (to distinguish from strings in String Theory proper).\\n\\n**1st:** Time moves like a wavefront through these worldlines--SAT calls this wavefront *the time surface*.\\n\\n**2nd:** What we perceive as a fundamental particle is the intersection of the particle's worldline with the time wavefront.\\n\\n### Pillar Number One\\n\\nThe Standard Model of Particle Physics is the evolving three-dimensional structure of everything--from quarks to organisms to the entire observable universe, and probably beyond. The organizational structure of the universe can be viewed as braided threads, tangled yarns, thick ropes, and ultimately a vast complex and highly structured literal *fabric* of reality, and envisioning these structures and their interactions in four dimensions (or scaled down to three) may give useful intuitive insights into actual physical phenomena.\\n\\n**Proposition A:** Unless forced to do otherwise by evidence or the internal logic of SAT, the theory will treat the entirety of the Standard Model of Particle Physics as essentially accurate, and will consider it fully imported into the theory with little or no change, apart from conceptual translation into the geometry of SAT.\\n\\n**3rd:** There must be a real interaction between the time wavefront and these worldlines--a transfer of energy from the wavefront to the worldlines, vice versa, or (most likely), both.\\n\\n**4th:** These interactions govern particle formation and stability.\\n\\n**5th:** These interactions must exert a force back on the wavefront as well.\\n\\n**6th:** This back-transmission of energy from the filament network (Zottenwelt) creates curvature of the time surface.\\n\\n### Pillar Number Two\\n\\nThe back-pull of the filament structure on the time surface creates curvatures of the time surface that re-create the curved spacetime of General Relativity very naturally from within SAT.\\n\\n**Proposition B:** Unless forced to do otherwise by the evidence or the internal logic of the theory, SAT will treat General Relativity as essentially correct, and *fully importable* into SAT's construction of the Standard Model of particle physics with little to no change beyond conceptual translations into the geometry of SAT.\\n\\n**7th:** The 4-dimensional extent of a particle's worldline and the time wavefront are physical, not just conceptual or historical objects and therefore, the forces these fundamental structures exert upon one another are quite likely transfered along each filament's extension in the fourth-dimensional extent of the filaments, both forward (in the direction of the wavefront's travel, \\\"futureward\\\"), and backward (in the opposite direction, \\\"pastward\\\"), creating both the possibility the future affecting the present just as the past affects the future. However: See the 8th Fundamental Intuition.\\n\\n**Proposition C:** The structure and properties of these fundamental structures (filaments and the time surface) create an intuitive way to understand the limits of these \\\"backbleed\\\" effects; that is, filaments experience tensions, have tensile strength and limitations on their flexibility, and the same should be true of the time surface--thus, backward-propogation in time is structurally self-limiting by the geometry of SAT, the backbleed effects of any tension exerted by interactions in the future-direction are in a sense \\\"baked in\\\" to every interaction as it happens. This would naturally prevent causality violations except perhaps on a very fine--perhaps quantum--scale. This could account for the \\\"wierd\\\" and intuition-breaking implications of quantum physics.\\n\\n### Pillar Number Three\\n\\nUnless forced to do otherwise by the evidence or the internal logic of the theory, SAT will treat the enirety of quantum mechanics as essentially correct, and fully importable into the theory, apart from conceptual translation into the geometry of SAT.\\n\\n**Prime General Prediction Pathway:** The tensions exerted upon the past by the future and the future by the past are essentially not accounted for in the Standard Model, General Relativity, or Quantum Mechanics, and this blind spot is likely to produce observable anomolies in the actual behavior of physical systems in the world.\\n\\n**8th:** Known observational deviations from the Standard Model, General Relativity, and Quantum Mechanics may be explainable by general principles derived intuitively from the geometry of SAT.\\n\\n**9th:** The nature of the interaction between the time surface and filaments likely encode all of the properties observed in real world particle systems in ways that directly map onto the particle properties and families described by the Standard Model of Particle Physics. As the worldlines of particles (as \\\"hard-coded\\\" into filaments) would likely create complex patterns and structures at the point of intersection with the time surface, it is probable that particle behaviors are described by their intersectional geometry with the wavefront; e.g. the gross or absolute angle of intersection (labeled theta_4) is currently considered to be a primary contributor to imparting mass as an energetic transfer to the filaments from the wavefront--grossly speaking, the greater the angle, the more energy imparted, and the more mass instantiated at the intersection.\\n\\n### Pillar Number Four\\n\\nThe exact geometry of intersection depends also upon the behavior of the filaments; SAT currently treats them as analagous to vibrating guitar strings; the intersectional traces, projected over time of the contact with the wavefront and any given filament should produce helical patterns with variable dimensions and degrees of complexity; this is how SAT interprets the particle interaction laws described by the standard model--for example, quantum chromodynamics interactions are likely to be the result of a bi- and tri-partite limitation on the geometry, possibly modelable by physical coil- or twist-locking mechanisms, spin and flavor are likely mappable to other geometric morphologies present in the SAT geometry. Identifying the structures implicit in this intuition should give new key insights into relationships between the properties that govern the behaviors of particles.\\n\\n**10th:** Fundamental physical constants should be natural and intuitive implications about the structure and properties of the SAT geometry or phenomena arising emergently therefrom. For example, the Fine Structure Constant may be an absolute or average tensional limit on the transfer of force from the time surface to the filament network, or a limitation on the torsional limits of the filaments themselves. The Planck Constants should be similarly mappable. Identifying the structural implications of the SAT geometry should provide key insights into the nature and value of these, and other constants.\\n\\n**Proposition D:** Light, along with other forces modeled by force-carrying particles (bosons) in the Standard Model, is likely not truly particulate in nature, but rather phenomena that arise from force-transfer across the filament network by the (fermionic) filaments themselves. SAT currently models light as a sort of \\\"energy transfer release valve\\\" triggered by the absorption of more energy from the time wavefront than the filament's structures and properties can tolerate; a ripple in the filament network.\\n\\n**Proposition E:** Because mass is considered to be proportional or approximately proportional to a filament's angle of intersection with the time surface (theta_4), it is proposed that the vacuum of space too is filled with an aligned lattice of filaments whose angle of intersection is near-zero or otherwise very low compared to the filaments that give rise to mass-bearing particles. The low-misalignment allows the time surface to pass with little to no transfer of energy from the time surface to the aligned vacuum filament network.
